newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists want talks on early election.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists want talks on early election.

text.p: Bulgaria's beleaguered ruling Socialists, warning of an explosive political situation and a collapsing economy, appealed on Wednesday for talks with opposition parties to fix a date for early elections.

Interior minister Nikolai Dobrev, who is trying to form a government, said opposition parties must understand the depth of the crisis and he tried to woo them into talks by saying his government should function for just three to five months.

"The chaos and power vacuum may cause a threat to civil peace," he said in the interview on state television. "The deadlock is so complicated and the confidence in the government so low that the only alternative is new elections."
Dobrev, accused by anti-government protesters of unleashing riot police during a January 10 clash, said he was willing to stand aside and let another Socialist form the new cabinet.
After reciting a dire list of Bulgaria's economic woes, he called on politicians from all parties to "sit around the table and negotiate a date for elections."

The ex-communist Socialists have run a caretaker government since December 21 when prime minister Zhan Videnov quit. With the economy in a freefall, Bulgaria has been swept by 24 days of anti-government protests by students and opposition groups demanding immediate elections.
The lev has plunged, inflation has soared and President Petar Stoyanov has warned Western countries that Bulgaria may have to default on its $10 billion foreign debt.
Dobrev was given a mandate this week to form a new cabinet and he appeared to reject repeated calls by opposition parties to surrender the mandate and hold elections.
He said the country needed a technical government based on a broad coalition to carry out urgent economic reforms but he stressed this should be under "a Socialist mandate".
Dobrev's insistence that the Socialists must controll the interim government before elections was quickly rebuffed by the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF).
"There is only one condition under which we will agree to negotiate and that is if Dobrev agrees to give up the mandate," UDF deputy Assen Agov told Reuters.
"None of these proposals is acceptable, neither to the opposition nor to those on the streets," he added.
In his interview, Dobrev painted a bleak picture of the economy and admitted that the previous Socialist government, elected to a four-year term in December 1994, had failed.
"The present government crisis has released energy which was pent up before and we see the justified dissatisfaction in the protests," he said.
